source_text: Λέγω δὲ τοῦτο οὐκ ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ ἐξηγουμένου δύναμιν ἀναφέρων, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τὴν χάριν τῶν γεγραμμένων, φυσικῶς ἔχουσαν τὸ εὐπαράδεκτον, καὶ πάσῃ καρδίᾳ προσηνές τε καὶ φίλον, τῶν τὸ ἀληθὲς τοῦ πιθανοῦ προτιμώντων· Καθὸ καὶ ὁ ψαλμῳδὸς ἐμφατικώτατα τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας ἡδὺ παριστῶν, Ὡς γλυκέα, φησὶ, τῷ λάρυγγί μου τὰ λόγιά σου, ὑπὲρ μέλι τῷ στόματί μου. Χθὲς τοίνυν, καθόσον ἦν δυνατὸν, τῇ περὶ τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ διατριβῇ τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν εὐφράναντες, πάλιν ἀπηντήσαμεν σήμερον ἐν δευτέρᾳ ἡμέρᾳ, τῶν τῆς δευτέρας ἡμέρας ἔργων τὰ θαύματα κατοψόμενοι. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ οὐ λέληθέ με, ὅτι πολλοὶ τεχνῖται τῶν βαναύσων τεχνῶν, ἀγαπητῶς ἐκ τῆς ἐφ' ἡμέραν ἐργασίας τὴν τροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς συμπορίζοντες, περιεστήκασιν ἡμᾶς, οἳ τὸν λόγον ἡμῖν συντέμνουσιν, ἵνα μὴ ἐπὶ πολὺ τῆς ἐργασίας ἀφέλκωνται. Πρὸς οὓς τί φημι; Ὅτι τὸ δανεισθὲν τῷ Θεῷ τοῦ χρόνου μέρος οὐκ ἀφανίζεται, ἀλλὰ σὺν μεγάλῃ ἀποδίδοται παρ' αὐτοῦ τῇ προσθήκῃ. Καὶ γὰρ ὅσαι περιστάσεις ἀσχολίας ποιητικαὶ, ταύτας ὁ Κύριος παραπέμψει· καὶ σώματι τόνον, καὶ ψυχῇ προθυμίαν, καὶ συναλλαγμάτων εὐμάρειαν, καὶ τὴν εἰς πάντα τὸν βίον εὐοδίαν τοῖς τὰ πνευματικὰ προτιμότερα ποιουμένοις διδούς. Κἂν ἐν τῷ παρόντι δὲ μὴ κατ' ἐλπίδας ἡμῖν ἐκβῇ τὰ σπουδαζόμενα, ἀλλὰ πρός γε τὸν ἐφεξῆς αἰῶνα ἀγαθὸς θησαυρὸς ἡ διδασκαλία τοῦ Πνεύματος. Ἄνελε τοίνυν τῆς καρδίας πᾶσαν τοῦ βίου μέριμναν, καὶ ὅλον μοι σεαυτὸν ἐνταῦθα συνάγαγε. Οὐ γὰρ ὄφελός τι τῆς τοῦ σώματος παρουσίας, τῆς καρδίας σου περὶ τὸν γήϊνον θησαυρὸν πονουμένης. 3.2 Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς γενηθήτω στερέωμα ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ ὕδατος, καὶ ἔστω διαχωρίζον ἀνὰ μέσον ὕδατος καὶ ὕδατος. Ἤδη καὶ χθὲς ἠκούσαμεν Θεοῦ ῥημάτων, Γενηθήτω φῶς. Καὶ σήμερον, Γενηθήτω στερέωμα. Πλέον δέ τι ἔχειν δοκεῖ τὰ παρόντα, ὅτι οὐκ ἀπέμεινεν ὁ λόγος ἐν ψιλῷ τῷ προσ τάγματι, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν καθ' ἣν ἐπιζητεῖται τοῦ στερεώματος ἡ κατασκευὴ προσδιώρισεν. Ἵνα διαχωρίζῃ, φησὶν, ἀνὰ μέσον ὕδατος καὶ ὕδατος. Πρῶτον μὲν οὖν ἀναλαβόντες ζητῶμεν, πῶς ὁ Θεὸς διαλέγεται. Ἆρα τὸν ἡμέτερον τρόπον, πρότερον μὲν ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν πραγμάτων τύπος ἐγγίνεται τῇ νοήσει, ἔπειτα μετὰ τὸ φαντασθῆναι, ἀπὸ τῶν ὑποκειμένων τὰς οἰκείας καὶ προσφυεῖς ἑκάστου σημασίας ἐκλεγόμενος ἐξαγγέλλει; εἶτα τῇ ὑπηρεσίᾳ τῶν φωνητικῶν ὀργάνων παραδοὺς τὰ νοηθέντα, οὕτω διὰ τῆς τοῦ ἀέρος τυπώσεως, κατὰ τὴν ἔναρθρον τῆς φωνῆς κίνησιν, ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ νόημα σαφηνίζει; Καὶ πῶς οὐ μυθῶδες τῆς τοιαύτης περιόδου λέγειν τὸν Θεὸν χρῄζειν πρὸς τὴν τῶν νοηθέντων δήλωσιν; Ἢ εὐσεβέστερον λέγειν, ὅτι τὸ θεῖον βούλημα καὶ ἡ πρώτη ὁρμὴ τοῦ νοεροῦ κινήματος, τοῦτο Λόγος ἐστὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ; Σχηματίζει δὲ αὐτὸν διεξοδικῶς ἡ Γραφὴ, ἵνα δείξῃ ὅτι οὐχὶ γενέσθαι μόνον ἐβουλήθη τὴν κτίσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ διά τινος συνεργοῦ παραχθῆναι ταύτην εἰς γέννησιν. Ἐδύνατο γὰρ, ὡς ἐξ ἀρχῆς εἶπε, περὶ πάντων ἐπεξελθεῖν, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν· εἶτα, Ἐποίησε φῶς· εἶτα, Ἐποίησε τὸ στερέωμα· νῦν δὲ τὸν Θεὸν προστάττοντα καὶ διαλεγόμενον εἰσάγουσα, τὸν ᾧ προστάσσει καὶ ᾧ διαλέγεται κατὰ τὸ σιωπώμενον ὑποφαίνει, οὐ βασκαίνουσα ἡμῖν τῆς γνώσεως, ἀλλ' ἐκκαίουσα ἡμᾶς πρὸς τὸν πόθον, δι' ὧν ἴχνη τινὰ καὶ ἐμφάσεις ὑποβάλλει τοῦ ἀπορρήτου.
thought_title: The Word of God and the Firmament's Purpose
orientation: Basil is opening his third homily, on the firmament, and has just addressed the crowd, including artisans who want him to keep the sermon short.
pass_a_gloss: But I say this not referring to the power of the one expounding, but to the grace of the things written, which naturally has the quality of being readily received, and is pleasant and dear to every heart of those who prefer the true to the persuasive. Just as also the psalmist, most emphatically presenting the sweetness that comes from truth, says, 'How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey to my mouth.' Yesterday then, insofar as it was possible, having gladdened your souls with the occupation concerning the words of God, we have met again today on the second day, to behold the wonders of the works of the second day. But indeed it has not escaped my notice that many craftsmen of the manual trades, lovingly procuring their food for themselves from their daily work, have surrounded us, who shorten the discourse for us, so that they may not be drawn away from their work for long. To them what do I say? That the portion of time lent to God is not destroyed, but is repaid by him with great interest. For whatever circumstances produce busyness, these the Lord will send away; and he gives to the body vigor, and to the soul eagerness, and ease in dealings, and prosperity in the whole of life to those who make spiritual things more important. And even if in the present the things we are eager for do not turn out for us according to our hopes, yet for the age to come the teaching of the Spirit is a good treasure. Remove then from your heart every care of life, and gather your whole self here to me. For there is not any benefit of the body's being present, when your heart labors over the earthly treasure. 3.2 And God said, 'Let a firmament come to be in the midst of the water, and let it be separating between water and water.' Already yesterday we heard the words of God, 'Let light come to be.' And today, 'Let a firmament come to be.' But the present words seem to have something more, because the word did not remain in the bare command, but also defined in addition the reason for which the construction of the firmament is required. 'So that it may separate,' he says, 'between water and water.' First then, taking it up, let us inquire how God converses. Is it in our manner, that first the impression from the things comes to be in the thought, then after it has been imagined, choosing from the underlying things the proper and fitting significations of each, he declares them? Then, having handed over the things thought to the service of the vocal organs, thus through the impression on the air, according to the articulate movement of the voice, he makes clear the thought in the hidden mind? And how is it not mythical to say that God needs such a circuit for the declaration of the things thought? Or is it more pious to say that the divine will and the first impulse of the intellectual movement, this is the Word of God? But Scripture shapes him in a discursive way, in order to show that he not only willed the creation to come to be, but also that it be brought into generation through some co-worker. For it was possible, as he said from the beginning, to go through all things: 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth'; then, 'He made light'; then, 'He made the firmament.' But now, introducing God commanding and conversing, it hints at the one whom he commands and with whom he converses, according to what is left silent, not begrudging us the knowledge, but kindling us toward the desire, through which it suggests certain traces and indications of the ineffable.

choices.why: The adjective describes the natural quality of the written words as easy to accept; 'readily received' keeps the passive sense of the Greek compound.

choices.english: the sweetness that comes from truth
choices.why: The genitive ἀληθείας indicates source; 'that comes from truth' preserves the causal nuance.
The perfect of περιίστημι with accusative means to stand around someone; 'have surrounded' keeps the perfect aspect.

choices.term: τὸ δανεισθὲν τῷ Θεῷ τοῦ χρόνου μέρος
choices.english: the portion of time lent to God
choices.why: The aorist passive participle δανεισθέν means 'lent'; the genitive τοῦ χρόνου is partitive, so 'portion of time' is precise.
In the context of repayment, προσθήκη means an addition beyond the principal, i.e., interest; 'interest' captures the financial metaphor Basil is using.
The adverb describes the manner of Scripture's presentation as extended and detailed; 'in a discursive way' preserves the sense of a drawn-out narrative.

pass_b_english: I say this not to point to the power of the one expounding, but to the grace of what is written, which by its nature is readily received and is gentle and dear to every heart among those who prize truth above persuasion. The psalmist shows this sweetness that comes from truth most emphatically when he says, “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118:103 (LXX; Hebrew 119:103)). Yesterday, then, as far as we could, we gladdened your souls by dwelling on the words of God, and today we have met again on the second day to behold the wonders of the second day’s works. But I have not failed to notice that many craftsmen of the manual trades, who lovingly earn their food from their daily labor, have surrounded us and are shortening our discourse so that they are not drawn away from their work for long. What do I say to them? That the portion of time lent to God is not lost, but is repaid by him with great interest. For whatever circumstances produce distraction, the Lord will let these pass by, giving bodily strength, eagerness of soul, ease in dealings, and prosperity through the whole of life to those who make spiritual things their priority. And even if in the present our earnest efforts do not turn out according to our hopes, still for the age to come the teaching of the Spirit is a good treasure. So remove from your heart every care of life, and gather all of yourself here to me. For there is not any benefit in the body’s being present while your heart labors over an earthly treasure.

And God said, “Let a firmament come into being in the midst of the water, and let it separate water from water” (Genesis 1:6). Yesterday we already heard the words of God: “Let light come into being” (Genesis 1:3). And today: “Let a firmament come into being.” But the present words seem to have something more, because the word did not remain in the bare command alone, but also defined in addition the reason for which the construction of the firmament is required. “So that it may separate,” he says, “between water and water.” First, then, let us take up the question of how God speaks. Is it in our manner—first the impression from things arises in the understanding, then after imagining it, he selects from the underlying realities the proper and fitting signs of each and declares them, then hands over what has been understood to the service of the vocal organs, and so through the impression made on the air, by the articulate movement of the voice, makes the thought known secretly? And how is it not mythical to say that God needs such a roundabout way for the declaration of what he has understood? Or is it more reverent to say that the divine will and the first impulse of the intellectual movement—this is the Word of God? Scripture shapes him in a discursive way in order to show that he not only willed the creation to come into being, but also that it was brought into being through some co-worker. For it could have, as it said from the beginning, gone through all things: “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1); then, “He made light”; then, “He made the firmament.” But now, by introducing God commanding and speaking, it hints at the one to whom he commands and to whom he speaks, in what is left silent—not begrudging us the knowledge, but kindling us toward desire, through the traces and indications it suggests of the ineffable.

problems.source_quote: Ὡς γλυκέα, φησὶ, τῷ λάρυγγί μου τὰ λόγιά σου, ὑπὲρ μέλι τῷ στόματί μου
problems.why: Basil follows LXX numbering; this is LXX Psalm 118, not 119.
problems.ruling: LXX Psalm 118:103; English cites 119, wrong numbering for this Greek text.

problems.quote: who earn their food with difficulty
problems.source_quote: ἀγαπητῶς ἐκ τῆς ἐφ' ἡμέραν ἐργασίας τὴν τροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς συμπορίζοντες
problems.why: ἀγαπητῶς means 'dearly'/'with love,' not 'with difficulty'; misread or wrong sense.
problems.fix: who lovingly earn their food from their daily labor
problems.ruling: ἀγαπητῶς means 'gladly'/'willingly'; 'with difficulty' is wrong sense, changes meaning.

problems.quote: the Lord will send them away
problems.why: παραπέμψει means 'will let pass by'/'will overlook,' not 'send away'—sense of allowing to pass, not dismissing.
problems.fix: the Lord will let these pass by
problems.ruling: παραπέμψει means 'will let pass/overlook'; 'send away' changes meaning of God's action.

problems.why: ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ is adverbial 'in secret'/'secretly,' not 'the hidden thought'—refers to making thought known secretly/hiddenly, not a hidden thought as object.
problems.ruling: ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ is adverbial 'in secret'; English 'the hidden thought' misreads grammar, changes meaning.

edits.old: who earn their food with difficulty
the Lord will send them away
edits.new: the Lord will let these pass by

fixed: Psalm 119:103: Basil follows LXX numbering; source is LXX Psalm 118, so corrected to Psalm 118:103 (LXX; Hebrew 119:103).
who earn their food with difficulty: source ἀγαπητῶς means 'lovingly'/'dearly', not 'with difficulty'; corrected to 'who lovingly earn their food'.
the Lord will send them away: source παραπέμψει means 'will let pass by'/'will overlook', not 'send away'; corrected to 'the Lord will let these pass by'.
the hidden thought: source ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ is adverbial 'secretly', not 'the hidden thought' as object; corrected to 'makes the thought known secretly'.

last_rejected.source_quote: Ὡς γλυκέα, φησὶ, τῷ λάρυγγί μου τὰ λόγιά σου, ὑπὲρ μέλι τῷ στόματί μου
last_rejected.why: Basil quotes LXX Psalm 118, but the citation says Hebrew 119:103; Hebrew is 119, but LXX is 118. The parenthetical is confusing: LXX 118 = Hebrew 119, so the citation should note LXX 118 = Hebrew 119, not imply LXX 118 and Hebrew 119 are different verses.
last_rejected.ruling: Parenthetical correctly identifies LXX 118 and Hebrew 119; standard notation, not misleading.

last_rejected.why: ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ means 'in secret' or 'secretly' as adverbial, but 'makes the thought known secretly' is awkward and misleading; it suggests secrecy rather than the hidden/internal process of thought becoming speech.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ naturally means 'secretly/hiddenly'; rendering within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the reason for which the construction of the firmament is required
last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν αἰτίαν καθ' ἣν ἐπιζητεῖται τοῦ στερεώματος ἡ κατασκευή
last_rejected.why: ἐπιζητεῖται is passive: 'the reason for which the construction of the firmament is sought/inquired after,' not 'required.' The English 'required' changes the sense from 'the reason one asks why' to necessity.
last_rejected.fix: the reason why the construction of the firmament is sought
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιζητεῖται can mean 'sought/required'; 'required' fits context of why firmament's construction is demanded.

last_rejected.why: συνεργοῦ here refers to the Logos/Son as co-worker with the Father in creation; 'some co-worker' is too vague and indefinite, diminishing the theological specificity. The context reveals this is the Only-Begotten.
last_rejected.ruling: τινος συνεργοῦ is deliberately indefinite; source says 'some co-worker,' translator shouldn't add theology not explicit here.
